account:
It is day 1, just after seven in the morning, and I am in the town hall with the secretary and builder. Today's recorded business includes office at eight, grain inspection at the east-bank mill at ten, lunch at home at noon, council letters at one, tea with the neighbour at three, office at half past four, and home at seven. The secretary has confirmed the first three appointments, but I have not yet obtained the appointment book to reread it this morning. The office chest instead contained public works instructions, town accounts, and freight's services proposal; I saw the secretary remove the appointment book yesterday, so its absence need not be suspicious.

The unusual matters remain poorly substantiated. My notes record a crossing rumour originating with Townsfolk 02 and 22, neither of whom supplied details. Freight denied knowing about it. There are also questions about bakery lights: the neighbour could not identify who installed them or when. I do not know whether these matters are connected, who else is involved, or what purpose any unreported activity serves. Ordinary transport or lighting work is possible, but I have no evidence establishing an explanation.

There is a separate, documented public-works matter. Yesterday I directed the builder to inspect the bridge and public street lighting and provide specific defects and an itemized estimate, without authorizing paid work. This morning the builder asked whether repairs should be commissioned rather than reporting findings; the secretary has just asked him directly for his inspection report or estimate. That leaves the inspection's completion uncertain. Freight's proposal remains filed without authorization, and the secretary reported no correspondence requiring a decision yesterday evening. I should distinguish these ordinary pending matters from rumours, obtain firsthand findings, and keep today's appointments rather than assume a secret scheme.
